status_reason: Newtonian mechanics: no horizontal force in vacuum and negligible gravity from a small asteroid.

status_reason: A ship's gravity is negligible; released ordnance co-moves with the bomber absent a force.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

status_reason: No plausible field in open space produces ballistic arcs of that curvature; light-speed beams are straight.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

status_reason: Newton's first law and absence of aerodynamic lift in vacuum.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

status_reason: Impact-speed argument is sound, but very large low-density slabs could fragment and decelerate differently; intact km-scale pieces remain implausible.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

status_reason: Mean free paths in interplanetary space are astronomical-unit scale; no audible sound propagates.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
work: Star Wars: Episode I - The Phantom Menace

critique: Melting ~2.7 kg of aluminum in 11.5 s needs ~2.3x10^5 W (~300 hp); a lithium-ion battery would need ~3.3 m^3 for realistic run time, so a hilt-sized power source would require nuclear or antimatter energy densities (~2x10^13 J/m^3).
status_reason: Calorimetry and battery energy densities are well established; no chemical battery comes close.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
work: Star Wars: Return of the Jedi
depiction: Lightsabers are called 'laser swords', clash like metal, and Vader's thrown saber spins about a point inside the blade.
critique: A laser blade would be invisible from the side, have no end, and pass through another beam; the effortful swings and the thrown saber's rotation about a center of mass in the blade imply the blade has mass, so it cannot be light.
status_reason: Photons don't collide appreciably in vacuum and a beam can't terminate; rigid-body rotation argument is correct.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

status_reason: Kinematics and human g-tolerance figures are standard (assuming the rope/harness could take the load).

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: In the trailer, Mando's phase-pulse blast sends a ~100 kg opponent flying across a cave while Mando stays planted on gravel.

status_reason: Newton's third law and Coulomb friction; μ≈2.4 on gravel is unrealistic.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: Mando's Amban rifle scope lets him see people through a building wall.
critique: Infrared (thermal) imaging cannot see through walls or even glass; radio or X-ray illumination/backscatter or muon-shadow methods could in principle image through walls, so the scope is plausible only as an active radar/X-ray device.
status_reason: Through-wall radar and backscatter imaging exist; thermal IR is blocked by walls and glass.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
work: Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker
depiction: A Xyston-class Star Destroyer's 'superlaser' blows up planet Kijimi in ~10 s, with fragments flying outward.
critique: Fragment speeds (~0.3 planet radii/s) imply ~7x10^35 J of kinetic energy, a power of ~7x10^34 W—over 10^8 times the Sun's luminosity—per ship; and a true laser beam would be invisible in space.
status_reason: Energetics far exceed Earth's ~2x10^32 J binding energy; invisibility of collimated beams in vacuum is correct.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

critique: Using the eye's ~0.02° resolution, a 2.9-km Resurgent-class destroyer at ~221–400 km subtends 0.4–0.75°, so it would genuinely be visible (unlike the 100-m ISS's shape); the scene is plausible.
status_reason: Small-angle geometry and ~1 arcmin human acuity are standard; a non-orbiting ship at that altitude would however need constant thrust.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: The generation ship Nauvoo is spun up to provide 0.1 g spin gravity in its drum after previously using thrust gravity, with one bridge.
critique: For 0.1 g at the drum radius the ship needs only ~0.6 rpm (0.063 rad/s); the spin-up seen on screen (0.00038 rad/s^2) is slower than the stated 30 s; and since thrust gravity and spin gravity point in perpendicular directions, the ship really needs separate 'floors'/bridges for each mode.
status_reason: Centripetal acceleration a=ω²R and the orthogonality of thrust vs spin 'down' are correct.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

critique: Praised as correct: by Newton's third law and momentum conservation, pushing Naomi away sends Holden the opposite way, and his tether lets the pair recover—a rare accurate portrayal of free-fall mechanics.
status_reason: Straightforward momentum conservation in free fall.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: Solomon Epstein, testing his new fusion drive, is pinned by high-g acceleration and cannot lift his arm to cut the engine.
critique: Thrust acceleration acts like an enhanced gravitational field: at ~8 g a 35 N arm 'weighs' ~284 N (64 lb), so being unable to reach the controls is physically realistic.
status_reason: Equivalence principle and human g-tolerance support the depiction.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

status_reason: Simple kinematics shows the displayed numbers don't match; prolonged 3–4 g for weeks does approach c.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

status_reason: a=ω²R arithmetic is correct.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

critique: Real rockets have thrust exceeding weight and accelerate continuously (Falcon 9 ~5 m/s^2); constant-velocity ascent is unrealistic, and reaching 192 m/s in 2.5 s implies ~78 m/s^2 (~9 g)—survivable but extreme.
status_reason: Rocket ascent profiles accelerate; kinematics is straightforward.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: A 'mysterious force' knocks the Moon from orbit so it spirals toward Earth, pulling oceans off the surface.
critique: A brief push only changes the Moon to an elliptical orbit; a crash requires nearly removing its orbital angular momentum; even with the Moon nearly touching, Earth's gravity beats the Moon's on surface water, though extreme tides and tidal stresses would wreck mountains and buildings.
status_reason: Orbital mechanics and tidal analysis are correct; Roche-limit breakup of the Moon would also occur.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: Terrorists sever the Galactic Empire's space elevator (Star Bridge) from its top station; the cable falls and wraps around the planet causing destruction.
critique: A 36,000-km cable needs extreme material strength; modeling the severed cable as co-rotating pieces, the lower part falls and wraps about a third of the way around the equator while higher pieces may end up in orbit as debris—so a full planetary wrap is not expected.
status_reason: Qualitative dynamics are right, but a non-tension, piecewise model is crude, and Trantor's parameters differ from Earth's.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: The hidden Mar-Vell space lab is located six years later using a set of orbital 'state vectors' (position and velocity).
critique: State vectors fully define a Keplerian orbit, but unmodeled forces like atmospheric drag (as on the ISS at 400 km) would make long-term prediction fail unless the lab reboosts; the numbers shown don't map neatly onto a real orbit.
status_reason: Orbit propagation uncertainty from drag and perturbations is real; state vectors are the standard representation.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: Thruster-powered heroes like Star-Lord and War Machine fly at constant velocity with thrust angled backward from their feet.
critique: Constant velocity requires zero net force, but a tilted thrust leaves an unbalanced horizontal component; drag is negligible at those speeds, and thrusters at the feet would also create torque that tips the flier over.
status_reason: Newton's first and second laws and rotational equilibrium.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: The Endurance spacecraft rotates to 'generate 1 g of gravity' for its crew.
critique: Spinning doesn't generate gravity, it creates apparent weight via centripetal acceleration; the trailer's spin rate (~0.59 rad/s) implies a radius of only ~28 m for 1 g, a small, fast-spinning ring.
status_reason: a=ω²R; ~5.6 rpm at 28 m is consistent with 1 g, though it is above comfort limits (Coriolis-induced motion sickness).

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
work: Star Wars (original trilogy: A New Hope / Return of the Jedi)

status_reason: An explosion's ejecta cannot accelerate outward after release; relativistic ejecta speeds would require absurd energies.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

status_reason: Square-cube law and helicopter payload figures are correct.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

status_reason: Qualitatively right (hypersonic speeds and heating), but Allain's model was admittedly rough; the actual jump altitude in the film is uncertain.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: Birds launched near planetoids feel gravity only inside a visible 'atmosphere' bubble and fly straight outside it.

status_reason: Gravity has infinite range and no friction acts in vacuum; the game's model is a deliberate simplification.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

critique: Not a true Lagrange point (the bodies don't orbit); a stable oscillation between two attractors works with constant-magnitude 'gravity' (~10 N/kg) but would not be stable under inverse-square gravity, confirming the game's non-Newtonian force law.
status_reason: With 1/r^2 forces the midpoint between two equal masses is an unstable saddle along the line joining them.

credentials: PhD in numerical relativity (Guelph-Waterloo Physics Institute / Perimeter Institute); staff scientist in computational physics, Los Alamos National Laboratory

credentials: PhD in numerical relativity (Guelph-Waterloo Physics Institute / Perimeter Institute); staff scientist in computational physics, Los Alamos National Laboratory

status_reason: Schwarzschild radius r=2GM/c^2 and the shell theorem are textbook results.

credentials: PhD in numerical relativity (Guelph-Waterloo Physics Institute / Perimeter Institute); staff scientist in computational physics, Los Alamos National Laboratory

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

status_reason: Relative-velocity addition applies to massive projectiles at these speeds (for true light-speed bolts it would not).

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: ~86-m-tall Jaegers leap, fall and get knocked through the air at human-like speeds.
critique: Under the same gravity, a geometrically scaled-up jump takes longer by the square root of the scale factor: a motion lasting 1.17 s for a human would take ~7.6 s for a Jaeger, so the films' fast-moving giants are unphysical (sped up because realistic timing would be boring).
status_reason: Free-fall time scales as sqrt(h/g); dynamic similarity requires slower motion for larger bodies.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: The Sovereign homeworld is a strangely shaped, non-spherical planet.

status_reason: Hydrostatic equilibrium rounds bodies above a few hundred km in size.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist

status_reason: Density and contact-pressure arithmetic is sound given mass conservation; the films are inconsistent about shrinking mass.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: Orbital rendezvous missions where thrusting along the orbit makes the craft go faster at the same radius and thrusting sideways changes radius without changing speed.
critique: Real orbits don't work this way: a prograde burn raises the opposite side of the orbit into an ellipse (and ultimately slows the craft), so the game's gravity model is non-Newtonian—fitted GM isn't even consistent across radii—making rendezvous artificially easy.
status_reason: Kepler/Newton orbital dynamics: tangential Δv changes orbital shape, not speed at fixed radius.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: In the trailer, the station sits '372 miles above the Earth' and debris and astronauts are swept backward as if pushed by air.
critique: At ~600 km the residual atmosphere is far too thin to drag astronauts back; once you grab a structure you'd simply stop, and the common intuition that knocked-off objects 'fall behind' an orbiting craft is a misconception.
status_reason: Thermospheric drag at 600 km produces micro-newton forces on a person, negligible over seconds.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: The Elysium habitat is a huge rotating torus giving Earth-like gravity.
critique: Measuring the spin (~0.017 rad/s) and requiring 1 g implies a radius of ~34 km (±13 km), consistent with the enormous station shown; large radius allows slow, comfortable rotation.
status_reason: a=ω²R; the depiction is self-consistent (structural strength aside).

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: Discovery One's crew live in a centrifuge inside the crew sphere producing Earth-like gravity.
critique: The centrifuge can be at most ~8 m in radius; at 1 g that requires fast rotation, giving a large head-to-foot gravity gradient and noticeable Coriolis effects, so spinning the whole long ship would be a better design.
status_reason: Gravity gradient and Coriolis effects scale inversely with radius; small centrifuges are problematic.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: TIE fighters carry large hexagonal side panels, often interpreted as solar panels powering ion engines.
critique: Even with ~40 m^2 of panels at 1 AU feeding an ion drive, a ~10,000 kg fighter would accelerate at only ~0.001 m/s^2, and the wide panels raise the moment of inertia, hurting maneuverability—so the panels can't plausibly power a dogfighter.
status_reason: Solar flux (~1.4 kW/m^2) and ion-thruster physics give tiny thrust-to-mass ratios.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: The Millennium Falcon dives toward the ground and sharply pulls up to level flight in the trailer.
critique: Undoing the camera rotation, a ~54° pull-up in 1.58 s at ~200 m/s requires ~115 m/s^2, i.e. ~12.6 g felt by passengers—enough to cause blackout without protection.
status_reason: Centripetal acceleration estimate and human g-tolerance (~9 g with g-suits) are standard.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: Starkiller Base drains a star's mass into the planet to power its weapon.
critique: With the star's mass absorbed, the planet migrates to the system's center of mass, its surface gravity rises ~300,000-fold (nearly a black hole if compressed to ~3 km), and conservation of angular momentum would spin it up to ~44 rev/s—enough to fling everyone off despite the added gravity.
status_reason: Momentum/angular-momentum reasoning is sound, but assumes the absorbed stellar matter carries the orbital angular momentum into planetary spin; a planet holding a solar mass would actually collapse.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: A blaster bolt hits a stormtrooper and knocks him back about a body length.
critique: Momentum conservation with ~35 m/s bolts implies a bolt mass of several kg (≥2.2 kg even at double speed), vs ~50 g for a .50-cal bullet; a magazine of 20 shots would weigh as much as a person and the shooter would get equal recoil.
status_reason: Momentum conservation; Newton's third law gives equal recoil to the shooter.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: The Hermes spacecraft rotates to give its crew 0.4 g (as in the novel).
critique: Measured spin from the trailer (~0.109 rad/s) combined with 0.4 g implies a radius of ~329 m—far larger than the ship appears, so the film's rotation rate and the stated gravity don't match.
status_reason: Arithmetic correct, but trailer CGI spin rates may not be meant literally; the inconsistency is real.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: An arriving alien mothership's gravity lifts buildings off the ground beneath it.
critique: For its gravity to beat Earth's on a building a few km below, the ship needs a mass of order 10^18 kg (like a 70-km asteroid) concentrated nearby—and such a field would pull up the ground, air and everything else too, not just buildings.
status_reason: Newtonian gravity acts on all mass equally; selective lifting is impossible.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
work: Rogue One: A Star Wars Story
depiction: The Hammerhead corvette rams and pushes a Star Destroyer, rotating it into another destroyer.
critique: A rigid-body model shows an off-center push gives both translation and rotation; reproducing the observed ~0.27 rad/s spin requires ~2x10^11 N of thrust—about 6,000 times a Saturn V—from a small corvette.
status_reason: Torque/moment-of-inertia analysis is standard; the implied thrust is absurd for the ship's size.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: Kirk drops the derelict USS Franklin off a cliff so it can reach 'terminal velocity' and start its engines; the ship falls at a steady speed and the HUD shows percent of terminal velocity.
critique: Falling ~900 m, the ship would accelerate rather than descend at the steady speed shown, and with air drag would reach only ~128 m/s—far from terminal velocity; he also flags (as a homework question) that the bridge crew don't behave as if in free fall.
status_reason: Free-fall and drag dynamics; occupants of a freely falling ship experience weightlessness.

credentials: PhD physics (NC State); associate professor of physics, Southeastern Louisiana University; WIRED Dot Physics columnist
depiction: Birds fired toward a planetoid speed up only to ~30 m/s and then coast at constant speed while still inside its gravity field.
critique: 1-D shots show a constant ~30 m/s^2 pull that switches off once the bird reaches ~30 m/s—an effective speed cap like terminal velocity, which has no basis in airless space where gravity would keep accelerating the bird.
status_reason: Without a medium there is no drag-limited terminal speed; gravitational acceleration continues.

credentials: PhD theoretical physics (King's College London); Appleton Professor of Natural Philosophy and professor of physics and astronomy, Dartmouth College
depiction: A procedurally generated universe of ~18 quintillion planets, many detailed with flora and fauna, with a journey toward a mysterious galactic center.
critique: The game draws on real facts (vast numbers of galaxies, stars and planets) but for consistency most worlds should be barren since life is an exceedingly rare property of matter; and real galactic centers host supermassive black holes rather than mysteries—he questioned how consistent its 'dream-like worlds' would be with modern science.
status_reason: Supermassive black holes at galactic centers are established, but the rarity of life remains an open question, not a known fact.
